language.script_notes: Finnish is Uralic, not Germanic — long words, doubled vowels and consonants (aa, ää, kk), letters ä and ö but essentially no å in Finnish words. Street suffix -tie, company suffix 'Oy'. Bilingual Finnish/Swedish place-name signs on the south and west coasts; Northern Sámi in Lapland. .fi domain.

road_furniture.bollard_color: Black and white, similar palette to Sweden.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: Reads as cylindrical from the front — rounded rather than flat-faced, which separates it from Sweden's post. (Verify against current photos.)
road_furniture.line_paint: White edge lines. Centre-line colour is inconsistent in sources — historically yellow, with a shift toward white on newer roads — so treat centre-line colour as unreliable for Finland. Passing-place signs with arrows only are a Finland detail.
road_furniture.curb_style: No strongly distinctive curb style noted.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Wooden utility poles, some concrete. Minor direction signs are white text on blue with a bold filled arrow on the sides; warning signs have a narrow yellow border.

architecture.roof_style: Simple gabled roofs; no iconic national roofline.
architecture.roof_material: Profiled sheet metal and clay tile.
architecture.wall_construction: Painted timber panelling is very common in the countryside; brick and plaster in towns.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Falu/Falun red, mustard yellow and grey; generally muted.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Red wooden farmhouses and barns; small lakeside summer cottages (mökki). Cities carry functionalist and Alvar Aalto–era modernism, but that is not diagnostic.

nature.vegetation: Dense, remarkably uniform boreal forest of pine, spruce and birch covering most of the country.
nature.terrain: Notably flat — the highest point is only about 1,300 m, in the far north-western arm — and stippled with lakes (on the order of 180,000). Glacial ridges (eskers) and drumlins are the main relief.
nature.climate_signature: Snow-heavy Street View coverage and low winter sun. Long, straight forest roads, and gravel/dirt roads are more common than in Sweden or Norway — an unmarked Nordic gravel road is a good Finland bet.

vehicles.plate_color: White with the blue EU strip and 'FIN'.
vehicles.plate_format: Three letters, a hyphen, three digits (ABC-123).
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Older cars are common. Reindeer warning signs and free-roaming reindeer appear in Lapland.

google_coverage.blur_style: Standard Google blurring, nothing unusual noted.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: White Google car. Heavy winter and snow coverage; large stretches of near-identical forest road with few landmarks.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Falu-red houses, snow-heavy coverage, black-and-white bollards, Nordic road furniture, Swedish visible on bilingual signs
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Finnish text (doubled letters, -tie, Oy) is the instant tell versus Swedish. Finland is flatter, far more lake-covered, has more gravel roads, and its bollards look cylindrical rather than flat-faced.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Both languages are Uralic and look superficially similar; both flat, forested and Baltic
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Estonia has different plates (blue EU strip with 'EST'), warmer and less snowy coverage, more Soviet-era rural buildings, and southern European tree cover; Estonian uses õ and ü, Finnish does not.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Snowy Nordic coverage, conifer forest, wooden poles
confusion_set.tiebreaker: Norway is steep and fjord-cut with a yellow centre line; Finland is flat lake-and-forest. Norwegian text uses ø/æ and looks nothing like Finnish.
